title: Request fanout sampler + tokenizer triage
content:
Summary:
This note captures a focused triage we ran on CPU-side tail latency spikes during multi-request fanout (1 request triggering N downstream tokenization tasks). The pattern shows: moderate mean latency but elevated 95/99p under bursty arrival. We suspected a mixture of Python GIL contention, excessive request parsing/tokenization calls, and inefficient threadpool sizing.

Hypotheses:
- High fanout multiplies short-lived Python work (parsing + tokenization) causing frequent GIL grabs and scheduler churn.
- Tokenizer implementation does a lot of small allocations and codec conversions (utf8 decode, detokenizer heuristics), making it CPU-bound in userspace (not syscalls) for typical inputs.
- Threadpool size vs. core count mismatch causes context-switching and queuing; default pool too small for burst concurrency so requests pile up, then many wake up and contend.

Methodology / Tools used:
- Sampling profiler (py-spy) on live replica during controlled burst replay.
- perf top to get kernel vs user percentages.
- eBPF stack traces for latency-correlated request IDs (bcc/tethered).
- Lightweight synthetic harness: replayed production-like traces (p90 interarrival) against single replica with constant QPS.
- Instrumented tokenization to report microsecond-level timings and allocation counts.
- End-to-end latency histogram collection (Prometheus summaries) with trace ids.

Key Observations:
- py-spy samples: ~40% time in tokenize() path, 18% in request parsing (json.loads), 12% in await scheduling/gc. Small but frequent frames in unicode decoding.
- perf: user-space dominated (~92% user), syscall overhead negligible.
- eBPF traces: large fanout cases show many greenlet/async-wakeup events clustered when bursts end -> wake storms.
- Threadpool sizing: default pool(8) on 16-core machine led to queuing; bumping to 32 reduced queueing but increased context switch rates.

Microbenchmarks (single-request CPU cost, median of 10k runs):
- json.loads(request) + header parsing: 120-180us (varies with metadata size)
- tokenizer.encode(text) (py tokenizer): 250-700us (200 chars -> ~320us; 1k chars -> ~710us)
- utf8 decoding + normalization: ~40-80us per call
- subprocess RPC roundtrip (local unix socket) to rust-tokenizer daemon: ~90-130us (includes serialization)

Experiments and results:
1) Offload tokenizer to a small persistent process pool (Rust tokenizer via unix socket, 4 procs):
   - Result: per-request tokenization CPU reduces ~60% in Python heap; overall 95p latency improved ~18% under 200rps bursts.
   - Tradeoffs: small serialization cost, need for process supervision + backpressure.
2) Pre-parse JSON in C extension (ujson) for common routes:
   - Result: ~30% reduction in request parsing time; 95p improved marginally when parsing was dominant.
   - Risk: behavior differences, edge-case inputs require testing.
3) Increase threadpool to core*2 and use affinity pinning:
   - Result: lower queue lengths but CPU context-switch rate increased; best tradeoff at pool=cores*1.25 on our machines.
4) Python subinterpreters (py 3.11) prototype for tokenizer island:
   - Result: promising lower GIL interference in microbench; engineering cost high and some C-extensions incompatible.
5) Prefix cache for popular prompts (LRU, TTL 60s):
   - Result: cache hit reduces tokenization to near-zero; reduced tokens generated and saved ~35% CPU overall for tested workloads.

Interim Recommendations (practical, low-risk first):
- Short-term (1–2 sprints):
  - Deploy rust-tokenizer daemon as opt-in: 2-4 per replica behind local unix socket; adapt worker_count via autoscaler.
  - Switch latency-sensitive routes to ujson for request parsing where schema is stable.
  - Implement prefix/LRU cache for top N prompts (configurable per route).
  - Tune threadpool: set default to min(max(cores, 8), cores*1.5) and enable optional pinning per replica.

- Medium-term (2–3 sprints):
  - Prototype Python subinterpreters for pure-Python tokenizer to measure real-world gains.
  - Add lightweight in-process instrumentation to emit per-request microtimes (parsing, tokenization, scheduling) to correlate with traces.
  - Add backpressure at ingress to limit instantaneous fanout; graceful degrade with queued hints.

- Long-term:
  - Consider shipping a small Rust tokenizer extension (pyO3) to avoid IPC costs and bypass frequent allocations; must audit for API compatibility.
  - Rework WANing of per-token allocations (reuse buffers, arena allocator for tokenization) in Python code-path.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much of the tokenizer cost is language-model dependent (tokenization rules vary by model)? Need per-model profiling.
- How do multi-tenant noisy neighbors affect observed gains with offload? Run stress tests with mixed workloads.
- Safety: ujson behavior differences may cause subtle failures in malformed inputs; need fuzz tests.

Action items / owners:
- Rafael: spin up rust-tokenizer daemon prototype and perf harness (due 2024-02-28).
- Marcus: add ujson alternative route config and run canary (due 2024-03-05).
- Priya: implement per-route prefix LRU cache and dashboard (due 2024-03-12).
- Elena: run cross-model tokenization matrix and produce perf table + recommended defaults (due 2024-03-08).

Notes to self / rough logs:
- Replays used request sample set from 2024-01-21 spike window (trace id: replay-20240121-3).
- py-spy flamegraph: s3://perf-artifacts/2024-02/pyfanout-replay-flame.svg (large tokenize() wedge).
- Remember to test with GC tuning (PYTHONMALLOC=malloc vs arenas) — small wins on allocation-heavy tokenizer.

Appendix (commands used):
- py-spy record -o out.svg --pid <pid> --native --rate 200
- perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -- sleep 10 && perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
- golang harness: ./replay --trace replay-20240121-3 --qps 150 --burst 250

If reviewers want, I can split this into three small PRD-style docs: 1) tokenizer offload plan, 2) threadpool tuning guide, 3) instrumentation additions.

-- Elena
